🚀 Feature
Caffe2 has whitelisting mechanism (facebookarchive/caffe2#228) to reduce final binary size which is very useful for mobile apps. However, in my opinion, it is not really convenient to list all files to be compiled and is more appropriate to do the opposite - blacklisting file to exclude from compilation. It is easier to know what you don't really need and can exclude than to know every file that you need or needed by others as dependency.
Also with blacklisting it is more probable that after updating from master user won't have problems when building new version - it will include all newly added files into build automatically, but with whitelisting list should be updated every time to include newly added files.
Considering that in general it is functionality duplication (all that is possible to archive with whitelist is achievable with blacklist and vice versa) but with better convenience, I am opening this proposal to discuss addition of this functionality. Or it might be more relevant to replace whitelisting with blacklisting to avoid functionality duplication.
I have implemented this change locally for my project and able to provide pull requests for both variants.
nodes.title: [caffe2] Add blacklist capability for smaller mobile binaries

Now that most of the heavy lifting of the PyTorch build happens in cmake, I'd like to see setup.py get substantially slimmed down and simplified, and in the process make it clearer how environment variables get propagated to cmake.
What lead me to report this bug is that I cannot build PyTorch on account of #14486. I want to disable NCCL build entirely, but NO_DISTRIBUTED=1 (the documented option) does not do this. I read setup.py and I see USE_NCCL. But this variable is not computed from an environment variable at all. I modify it so that it is respected. I discover cmake is still building NCCL. I find this is because USE_NCCL is not propagated to the cmake in build_pytorch_libs.sh. Nonsense.
Here's what I would like to see: Every cmake option that we advertise as option in the top-level CMakeLists.txt, should be toggleable in some way from setup.py in an officially documented (and hopefully intuitive) way. It should be hard for developers adding new flags to break this invariant. My suggestion is that setup.py respect and translate identically named environment variables into their cmake equivalents automatically. (It might be somewhat tricky to ensure that setup.py and CMakeLists.txt always stay in sync.)

🚀 Feature
I would request that torch.set_printoptions add a flag so that scientific notation can be enabled or disabled.
Motivation
PyTorch printing has a limitation: the end user cannot force scientific mode printing to be enabled or disabled. (Currently, sci_mode is chosen based on logic in _tensor_str.py.)
This would give end-users more control, and it would be an easy change.
Pitch
One possible implementation would involve adding a named argument sci_mode to set_printoptions. Perhaps:

sci_mode=None would allow sci_mode to be determined by the current logic (the current default)
sci_mode=True would force sci_mode to be True
sci_mode=False would force sci_mode to be False

This would be easy to implement: based on the argument, sci_mode in class _Formatter could be unaffected or forced to be True or False.
Alternatives
I'm open to other implementations that would satisfy the same problem.
For example, Numpy's suppress argument to its set_printoption affects the printing of scientific notation.  (Note: In my opinion, Numpy's approach (with suppress) is a bit harder to reason about than my proposal, above. My proposal is orthogonal to the other feature flags. I often consider orthogonality to be a desirable property when it comes to configuration.)
Additional context

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonality_(programming)

📚 Documentation for torch.mul()
The doc for torch.mul(tensor, tensor) is inaccurate.
There are two issues.

The doc says that


Each element of the tensor input is multiplied by each element of the Tensor other

i.e. a Cartesian product but then the doc provides the equation:

out_i = input_i * other_i.

and then the example provided in the doc does not match the math...
>>> a = torch.randn(4, 1)
>>> a
tensor([[ 1.1207],
        [-0.3137],
        [ 0.0700],
        [ 0.8378]])
>>> b = torch.randn(1, 4)
>>> b
tensor([[ 0.5146,  0.1216, -0.5244,  2.2382]])
>>> torch.mul(a, b)
tensor([[ 0.5767,  0.1363, -0.5877,  2.5083],
        [-0.1614, -0.0382,  0.1645, -0.7021],
        [ 0.0360,  0.0085, -0.0367,  0.1567],
        [ 0.4312,  0.1019, -0.4394,  1.8753]])


There is a case when the math is correct and the multiplication is the naive element-wise product.

>>> a
tensor([[ 0.6680,  0.6326],
        [-0.5282, -0.2136],
        [ 0.1368,  1.3523],
        [ 0.7610, -0.1188]])
>>> b
tensor([[-0.5711, -1.2996],
        [ 1.4009,  0.5595],
        [-0.6578,  0.9210],
        [-0.4245,  0.9258]])
>>> torch.mul(a,b)
tensor([[-0.3815, -0.8222],
        [-0.7400, -0.1195],
        [-0.0900,  1.2455],
        [-0.3231, -0.1100]])

IMHO a multiplication function that is sometime element-wise and sometime a matrix multiplication is open to undesired behavior if the user has an undetected issue with dimensions. Perhaps in the second case torch.mul() should complain about dimensions. But in any case the inconsistency should be documented.

🚀 Feature
CUDA 10 released a new feature called CUDA Graphs which allows you to build static graphs that can minimizes the overhead of launching multiple kernels. The API comes with functions that allow you to capture a stream (multiple streams are also supported) and transform it into a CUDA graph. Exposing this feature to pytorch can be very beneficial to many applications.
Motivation
When working with small kernels it is important to minimize any overhead without adding complexity.
Pitch
I propose something like:
g = CUDAGraph()
with g.capture():
    # Static computation that can be combined into 1 graph
    ....

while True:
    g.execute()

Alternatives
Currently Pytorch offers JIT, and C++ APIs that mitigate the overhead. The CUDA Graph approach is theoretically faster and IMHO more friendly to users.
Additional context
I have a small demo working where I run a small neural network 1000 times and here are the current benchmarks I have:
Pytorch c++ Front-end: 152.633ms
Pytorch c++ with cuda graphs capture:136.692ms
Pytorch Python: 354.79ms
Pytorch Python + cuda graphs capture: 134.29ms

🚀 Feature
Support for OSX SDK 10.9.
Motivation
OSX SDK 10.9 is used in Anaconda's default channels:
https://conda.io/docs/user-guide/tasks/build-packages/compiler-tools.html#macos-sdk
While there isn't a clear cut requirement for wheel files, it might be good to support an SDK a little older than 10.12.
Python.org installers are apparently built for OSX 10.9 in 3.7.

Up until Python 3.7, Python.org installers were built to be compapatible with macOS 10.6, and were dual architecture (i386 and x86_64 == 32- and 64- bit). Python.org Python 3.7 has an alternative installer compatible with Python 10.9 and above, and only containing x86_64 / 64 bit architecture.

See https://github.com/MacPython/wiki/wiki/Spinning-wheels
Pitch
I think the only patch that is needed is for clock_gettime.
A patch like this one might do, but the clock isn't really monotonic, so there might be unintended consequences when timezone changes occur.
diff --git a/torch/csrc/autograd/profiler.h b/torch/csrc/autograd/profiler.h
index 2fd623a43..0750cdff7 100644
--- a/torch/csrc/autograd/profiler.h
+++ b/torch/csrc/autograd/profiler.h
@@ -35,11 +35,21 @@ constexpr inline size_t ceilToMultiple(size_t a, size_t b) {
   return ((a + b - 1) / b) * b;
 }
 
+#if defined(__MACH__) && !defined(CLOCK_REALTIME)
+#include <sys/time.h>
+// clock_gettime is not implemented on older versions of OS X (< 10.12).
+// If implemented, CLOCK_REALTIME will have already been defined.
+#endif
+
 inline int64_t getTime() {
 #ifdef _WIN32
   using namespace std::chrono;
   using clock = std::conditional<high_resolution_clock::is_steady, high_resolution_clock, steady_clock>::type;
   return duration_cast<nanoseconds>(clock::now().time_since_epoch()).count();
+#elif defined(__MACH__) && !defined(CLOCK_REALTIME)
+  struct timeval now;
+  gettimeofday(&now, NULL);
+  return static_cast<int64_t>(now.tv_sec) * 1000000000 + static_cast<int64_t>(now.tv_usec) * 1000;
 #else
   // clock_gettime is *much* faster than std::chrono implementation on Linux
   struct timespec t{};
Alternatives
Keep supporting 10.12 only.

A few projects now implement the __cuda_array_interface__ protocol, which was originally designed by the Numba developers to enable clean operation on arrays managed by other projects.  I believe that today both PyTorch and CuPy have implemented this protocol, and that Numba is the only consumer.
However, libraries like PyTorch and CuPy could also identify this protocol on input objects and use it within their functions.  Probably the first use case would be to allow users to easily convert between different GPU array libraries.  For example, ideally the following would work.
import cupy
x = cupy.random.random((1000, 1000))

import torch
t = torch.tensor(x)
Ideally the check within torch.tensor would be something like the following:
if hasattr(x, '__cuda_array_interface__'):
    ...
rather than the following:
if isinstance(x, cupy.ndarray):
    ...
which would be useful for support of future GPU libraries.
xref #11914

🐛 Bug
The random sampler (torch.utils.data.RandomSampler) allows the user to define how many samples are drawn (when replacement is set to True). However the len method always returns the length of the dataset ad doesn't take this parameter into consideration.
Ideally when the user specifies the num_samples parameter, this value should be returned in the len method (right now the length of the sampler and returned iterator don't match if num_samples is set).
Since num_samples is anyway set to the length of datasource if not specified explicitly, the following is a simple fix:
def __len__(self):
    return self.num_samples

Tested with pytorch version 1.0
